content.text:
Every declaration now matches its sheet list, and the text follows the figures.

**What was wrong and what I did**

The preflight compared each brief's `**Numerals appearing on this figure:**` declaration against the sheet list at the foot of the same file. FIG. 1 declared 10, 36 and 44 while its sheet list called for 10, 12, 18, 20, 24, 36 and 44; FIG. 2 declared 18, which its sheet list does not carry. No numeral definition or specification text was deleted to fix this: the labels were put back on the sheets the plan assigns them to.

- **FIG. 1** now draws and labels the full set. The base 12 is the slab, targeted well inside its broad front face; the vibration motor 18 and the air-extraction mechanism 20 are the left and right housings on the top face, each targeted inside its broad front face; the perimeter member 24 is the band under the slab, whose front strip is specified deep enough to hold an interior point clear of the underside above and the tile below; the handle 44 is now a plain closed block rather than a ring, so it has a solid interior to label instead of an open area that previously attracted endpoints; the device 10 is targeted anywhere along the machine's outer silhouette, which distinguishes the whole assembly from the base without demanding a single corner line. Trimmed to 2795 characters after the additions.
- **FIG. 2** drops the vibration motor housing and numeral 18, leaving one housing, the air-extraction mechanism 20, and states that the motor and handle are omitted. The uniform hatching and the other endpoint targets are unchanged.
- **Text synchronization:** the Brief Description of the Drawings now lists for FIG. 1 the base, motor, air-extraction mechanism, perimeter member, handle and covering element, and for FIG. 2 records that the motor and handle are omitted. In the detailed description, the motor paragraph now reads that the vibration motor 18 is carried on the base 12 as seen in FIG. 1, so no passage points a reader to a sheet that no longer labels it.

Coverage after the move is intact: all 16 numerals in the table appear across the five sheets, no sheet carries more than seven, and every brief is under 2800 characters. FIGS. 3, 4 and 5 were untouched apart from the FIG. 4 clearance depth added earlier. No claim, numeral definition, or disclosed embodiment changed.

input.summary: Fixed the mechanical preflight failure: FIG. 1's numeral declaration was missing 12, 18, 20 and 24, and FIG. 2 declared 18, which is not on its sheet list. FIG. 1 now draws and labels all seven assigned numerals with broad interior targets, FIG. 2 drops the vibration motor housing and numeral 18, and the Brief Description of the Drawings and detailed description were re-synchronized so no passage sends a reader to a sheet that does not carry the part. No numeral definition, claim, or disclosed embodiment was deleted or changed.
reasoning: The failure was a figure-plan coverage mismatch, so the fix had to put labels back on their assigned sheets rather than trim the plan. FIG. 1's sheet list assigns 10, 12, 18, 20, 24, 36 and 44; the brief body had been reduced to three of them. I rebuilt the FIG. 1 geometry to carry all seven and left the sheet list untouched.

FIG. 1 previously failed endpoint review on exactly these numerals, so restoring them meant rebuilding the targets, not just re-listing them. The base 12 moved to the broad front face of the slab, which is a large interior region and is free of the housings and grip that stand on the top face where the endpoint kept drifting.

The device 10 and the base 12 now share a sheet, so their targets must be distinguishable. I made 10 a boundary target, anywhere along the machine's outer silhouette taken with slab, band, housings and grip together, and 12 an interior target. Interior versus boundary is a distinction the endpoint reviewers can verify, and dropping the earlier front-left corner-line requirement removes the over-specific constraint that failed before.

The handle 44 is now a plain closed block instead of a ring enclosing an open area. The open area of the ring was the region that attracted stray endpoints in the earlier report, and the disclosure specifies no handle shape, so the simplest generic outline is the correct depiction convention and gives a solid interior to label.

The perimeter member 24 endpoint had only 0.2 units of clearance in the rendered sheet, which is a geometry problem rather than a wording problem, so the brief now requires the band's front strip to be drawn deep enough for a point well inside it to clear the underside above and the tile below.

Removing 18 from FIG. 2 left the specification asserting that the motor is visible there, so I followed the numeral to FIG. 1 through the text: the Brief Description now records the motor as omitted from FIG. 2 and shown in FIG. 1, and the motor paragraph in the detailed description points to FIG. 1, which lists both 18 and 12.

Adding four numerals pushed FIG. 1 to 3068 characters, over the 2800 limit, so I cut length from rendering prose rather than from targets or relationships: redundant restatements of the slab boundaries and of the housing block description went, while every part, contact, and endpoint target stayed. The file is now 2795 characters.

I did not touch FIGS. 3 and 5 or the numeral table. Their declarations already match their sheet lists, and changing passing text to chase an unrelated failure would only put certified sheets back at risk.

New targets: 12 well inside the broad front face of the slab, 18 and 20 well inside their broad front faces, 24 well inside the front strip of the band which is specified deep enough to hold an interior point clear of the underside and the tile, 44 well inside the front face of the grip, 10 anywhere along the machine's outer silhouette. Declaration updated to 10, 12, 18, 20, 24, 36, 44 and trimmed to 2795 characters.

input.prior_art_strategy: Unchanged this turn; no claim, Background, or citation was touched, and the positions were re-verified rather than re-argued. Claim 1 stands on the combination of a rigid low-friction perimeter member that is deliberately not a seal, leaving a clearance along at least part of its length through which ambient air enters continuously, an air-extraction mechanism whose volumetric extraction rate holds the chamber below atmospheric pressure during that continuous ingress, and an all-rigid vibration transmission path from motor to bearing face with the bearing face slidable while the differential is maintained. That carries clear of DE-202021002652-U1, whose suction cups are each formed by a rubber-elastic apron; of US-11408462-B2, whose peripheral wall is elastic partitions with a rigidity frame added to stop the partition deforming into the decompressed space; of US-10001245-B2, which abandons the vacuum coupling and floats on an air cushion in blower mode in order to move; and of US-4934475-A, where vibration reduces the suction-adhering force and drives the body along the wall rather than being delivered into a laid covering element. US-11247858-B2 is a sheet-lifting vacuum plate that carries the article away from the work surface, and the Background states only that supported teaching and why it does not bear on holding a vibrating tool down on a covering element. All five keys are cited, in the Background only.

content.text:
Both findings are fixed inside the figure briefs; no application text changed.

**Numeral 10 convention (FIG. 5).** The assembly numeral now uses the same convention on both perspective sheets: it terminates on the machine's outer silhouette, the line at which the rectangular body and its band together stand against the open background, at any place along that line clear of the flexible pulling element 46. Interior faces remain reserved for the parts they belong to, so the leader for the whole device no longer lands in the region FIG. 1 identifies as the base 12.

**Handle placement (FIG. 1).** The paragraph describing the grip now states that the position of the grip on the slab, and its position relative to the two housings, are a placement convention for this sheet only and assert no particular mounting location. The disclosure says handles exist and what they are for but not where one attaches, so the drawing convention is now explicitly labelled as such. Nothing corresponding was added to the Brief Description of the Drawings or the detailed description, which stay position-neutral.

Two consequential adjustments were needed to keep the briefs legal after those additions. FIG. 1 rose to 2820 characters and FIG. 5 to 2847, both over the 2800 limit, so I recovered length from wording rather than content: shorter endpoint phrasing on FIG. 1 (each target still names the same part and the same broad region), and on FIG. 5 the removal of the cord's line-weight and single-stroke rendering instruction, which was a generic linework control. The cord is still specified as one slack curved path drawn as a single continuous curved line, which is what the drawing rules call for. FIG. 1 is now 2793 characters and FIG. 5 is 2748; all five briefs are under the limit, every declaration matches its sheet list, and all 16 numerals remain covered across the sheets.

input.summary: Applied both reviewer findings inside the figure briefs. FIG. 5's numeral 10 now uses the same outer-silhouette endpoint convention as FIG. 1, so the assembly leader no longer terminates on the region the application identifies as the base. FIG. 1 now states that the grip's position on the slab and relative to the two housings is a placement convention for that sheet only and asserts no mounting location. To stay within the 2800-character limit after those additions I shortened endpoint phrasing on FIG. 1 and removed a generic linework control from the FIG. 5 cord description. No claim, description, drawing description, or numeral definition changed.
reasoning: Both findings were about the briefs, and the reviewer supplied wording that resolves them without touching the specification, so I applied it rather than inventing a different cure that would have to be re-verified.

The numeral 10 inconsistency mattered because the two perspective sheets were making incompatible promises: FIG. 1 reserved the slab's front face for base 12 and routed 10 to the silhouette, while FIG. 5 routed 10 into the same visual region on a sheet where that body is the base with the motor and pump omitted. Making both sheets use boundary-for-assembly and interior-for-part gives the endpoint reviewers one rule to check across the drawing set.

The handle finding is a source-fidelity point, not an aesthetic one. The disclosure affirms that handles exist and that they guide rather than press, but never says where one attaches, so a brief that fixes the grip on the top face between the two housings was asserting an untraced mounting relationship. The existing schematic disclaimer covered only the rectangular shapes, so the placement convention had to be disclaimed in its own terms.

I deliberately kept that disclaimer out of draft/07-drawings.md and draft/08-detailed-description.md. Adding it to the specification would convert a drawing convention into disclosed subject matter, which is the opposite of what the finding asks for; the application text stays position-neutral at 'may include one or more handles 44, as shown in FIG. 1'.

The two additions pushed FIG. 1 to 2820 and FIG. 5 to 2847 characters, over the limit, so length had to come from somewhere. I took it from wording rather than substance: endpoint sentences on FIG. 1 now say 'well inside its front face' instead of restating the housing, which names the same part and the same broad region.

content.text:
All three sheets are repaired at the geometry level, where the endpoint failures actually originate.

**FIG. 1 (numerals 12 and 44 misplaced).** The two rejected targets were the thin front face of the slab and a small grip block competing with two similar housings. The sheet now draws three closed blocks standing side by side on the top face, named by stable position: the left-hand block is the vibration motor 18, the middle block is the grip, the right-hand block is the air-extraction mechanism 20, each with a broad front face drawn large enough for an interior point to clear its edges. The base 12 is now the large surface below all three blocks and above the band, and the slab is specified thick enough for a point well inside that face to clear its upper and lower edges. The handle 44 target is the middle block's front face, which is a stable positional reference rather than a shape the annotator has to find. The placement disclaimer added last turn is retained, so the grip's position still asserts no mounting location.

**FIG. 5 (numeral 24 misplaced).** The band's front surface is now specified as one unbroken strip running the whole width of the machine, deep enough for a point well inside it to clear the underside above and the tile below, and the numeral target is that interior surface. The same wording now governs the band on FIG. 1, so the perimeter member is labelled the same way on both perspective sheets.

**FIG. 3 (independent endpoint audit).** Both targets on this sheet sit inside a rectangular ring, so each region is now required to be wide enough to hold an interior point clear of its bounding edges: the band between the outer and inner rectangles, and the field within the inner rectangle. The perimeter member 24 target is anchored to the left-hand side of the ring, and the second side 16 target is the enclosed field clear of the band all round.

All five briefs are under the 2800-character limit (2795, 2591, 2161, 2768, 2793), each declaration still matches its sheet list, all 16 numerals remain covered across the sheets, and no claim, description, drawing description, or numeral definition was touched.

input.summary: Repaired the three failing sheets by enlarging the target regions and naming each target by a stable position rather than by shape. FIG. 1 now shows three side-by-side blocks on the top face (left is the vibration motor 18, middle is the grip, right is the air-extraction mechanism 20) over a thick slab whose front face is the largest surface on the machine, fixing the rejected endpoints for base 12 and handle 44. FIG. 5's band is specified as one unbroken full-width strip deep enough to hold an interior point, fixing numeral 24. FIG. 3 requires both the ring band and the enclosed field to be wide enough for an interior point clear of their edges, with 24 anchored to the left-hand side of the ring. No application text changed.
reasoning: All three failures were rejected coordinate clusters, which is a geometry problem rather than a wording problem. Restating the same target in new words would have produced the same thin region, so in each case I enlarged the region the renderer must draw and then pointed the numeral at it.

On FIG. 1 the base 12 target failed because the slab's front face is a narrow horizontal strip when the housings above it dominate the machine. The slab is now specified thick, with its front face the largest plain surface on the machine, running the whole width below the blocks and above the band, so the interior point has room.

The handle 44 target failed because a grip sitting between two similar housings is hard to single out. Naming the three bodies as left-hand, middle and right-hand blocks turns every top-face target into a positional reference, which is the disambiguation the drawing rules call for, and it removes any need for the annotator to identify a part by its shape.

I kept the placement disclaimer for the grip that the previous review required. Calling the grip the middle block is a page position, and the brief still says the position on the slab and relative to the other two blocks asserts no mounting location, so the positional naming does not smuggle back an untraced mounting relationship.

FIG. 5's numeral 24 and FIG. 1's numeral 24 label the same kind of thin skirt strip, so I gave both sheets the same specification: one unbroken strip running the whole width, deep enough for a point well inside it to clear the underside above and the tile below. Fixing only the sheet that failed would have left the other one waiting to fail.

FIG. 3's audit gave no numeral, and the sheet has only two targets, both inside a rectangular ring, so I treated both as suspect: the band and the enclosed field must each be wide enough to hold an interior point clear of their bounding edges. Anchoring 24 to the left-hand side of the ring replaces the vague 'at any place along it' with a named side while keeping a broad region.

Every enlargement is stated as schematic with no proportion asserted, because the disclosure gives no dimensions for the base, the perimeter member, or the tile. The depth requirements are depiction conventions for the sheets, not asserted structure.

The additions pushed FIG. 1 to 3117 characters and FIG. 5 over the limit, so I compressed wording rather than dropping content: redundant restatements of the blocks and the band went, and every part, contact, and target region survived. FIG. 1 is 2795 and FIG. 5 is 2793.

input.prior_art_strategy: Unchanged this turn; the repairs were confined to figure briefs and no claim or Background text was touched. Claim 1 still rests on the rigid low-friction perimeter member that is deliberately not a seal, leaving a clearance along at least part of its length through which ambient air enters continuously, an air-extraction mechanism whose volumetric extraction rate holds the chamber below atmospheric pressure during that continuous ingress, and an all-rigid vibration transmission path from motor to bearing face with the bearing face slidable while the differential is maintained. That combination carries clear of DE-202021002652-U1, whose suction cups are each formed by a rubber-elastic apron; of US-11408462-B2, whose peripheral wall is elastic partitions with a rigidity frame added to keep the partition from deforming into the decompressed space; of US-10001245-B2, which gives up the vacuum coupling and floats on an air cushion in blower mode in order to move; and of US-4934475-A, where vibration reduces the suction-adhering hold and drives the body along the wall instead of being delivered into a laid covering element. US-11247858-B2 is a sheet-lifting vacuum plate that carries the article away from the work surface, and the Background states only that supported teaching and why it does not bear on holding a vibrating tool down on a covering element. All five keys are cited, in the Background only.

**View:** Perspective view from above and to the front left. Outline line work only, with no lettering drawn.

**Geometry to be drawn**

The covering element 36 is one large plain tile in perspective, filling the lower part of the drawing area. The machine stands on its left-hand part, leaving a wide open expanse of tile to the right.

The machine is one plain rectangular slab, the base 12, standing on a band that runs round its underside. Three closed blocks stand side by side on the top face of the slab, clear of one another: the left-hand block is the vibration motor 18, the middle block is the grip, and the right-hand block is the air-extraction mechanism 20. Each has a broad front face turned toward the viewer, large enough for a point well inside it to stand clear of its edges. The whole of the drawing stands well inside the drawing area.

content.text:
The single reported defect is fixed.

**Terminology (FIG. 1).** The brief called the middle block "the grip" in the geometry paragraph and repeated that name in the placement disclaimer, while the label list, numeral table, drawing descriptions, detailed description, and claims 8 and 17 all call the same part "handle". The brief now reads "the middle block is the handle 44" and "the position of the handle 44 on the slab and relative to the other two blocks being a placement convention that asserts no particular mounting location". The part now has one name and one numeral everywhere it appears, and the placement disclaimer is otherwise unchanged.

To absorb the two longer names without breaking the length limit I shortened one phrase in the numeral 10 endpoint sentence, which still names the same silhouette boundary. FIG. 1 is 2796 characters; the other briefs are unchanged at 2591, 2161, 2768 and 2793. Every declaration still matches its sheet list, all 16 numerals remain covered across the five sheets, and no claim, description, drawing description, or numeral definition was touched.

input.summary: Fixed the one reported defect: the FIG. 1 brief called part 44 "the grip" in its geometry paragraph and placement disclaimer while every other file calls it the handle. Both occurrences now read "handle 44", so the part carries one name and one numeral throughout. One phrase in the numeral 10 endpoint sentence was shortened so the brief stays within the character limit. No application text, claim, or numeral definition changed.
reasoning: The finding was a one-part-two-names slip, exactly what the numeral table exists to prevent, so I took the reviewer's wording rather than inventing a third term. The brief now says 'the middle block is the handle 44' and 'the position of the handle 44 on the slab', matching draft/numerals.md, the drawing descriptions, the detailed description, and claims 8 and 17.

I checked whether 'grip' appeared anywhere else before editing. The other occurrences are in the Background, Summary, and detailed description, where the word is used for a suction cup gripping a tile and for the operator's grip, neither of which names part 44, so those are correct as they stand and I left them alone.

The positional naming that fixed the previous endpoint failure had to survive the rename. Calling the block 'the middle block' is what lets the annotator find it, so I kept that phrasing in both the geometry paragraph and the label bullet and changed only the part name.

The rename added ten characters and pushed FIG. 1 to 2805, over the 2800 limit, so I recovered length from the numeral 10 endpoint sentence by dropping a redundant word. The sentence still names the same silhouette boundary formed by slab, band and blocks, so no target region changed.

input.prior_art_strategy: Unchanged this turn; the edit was a terminology fix inside one figure brief and no claim or Background text was touched. Claim 1 still rests on the rigid low-friction perimeter member that is deliberately not a seal, leaving a clearance along at least part of its length through which ambient air enters continuously, an air-extraction mechanism whose volumetric extraction rate holds the chamber below atmospheric pressure during that continuous ingress, and an all-rigid vibration transmission path from motor to bearing face with the bearing face slidable while the differential is maintained. That combination carries clear of DE-202021002652-U1, whose suction cups are each formed by a rubber-elastic apron; of US-11408462-B2, whose peripheral wall is elastic partitions with a rigidity frame added to keep the partition from deforming into the decompressed space; of US-10001245-B2, which gives up the vacuum coupling and floats on an air cushion in blower mode in order to move; and of US-4934475-A, where vibration reduces the suction-adhering hold and drives the body along the wall instead of being delivered into a laid covering element. US-11247858-B2 is a sheet-lifting vacuum plate that carries the article away from the work surface, and the Background states only that supported teaching and why it does not bear on holding a vibrating tool down on a covering element. All five keys are cited, in the Background only.

content.text:
The one failing sheet is repaired.

**FIG. 1, numerals 12 and 44.** Both dots landed on a boundary line rather than inside a face: numeral 12 near the corner where the slab's front and left faces meet, numeral 44 on the top edge of the middle block's front face. The repair works on both halves of the problem.

Geometry: the machine is now drawn large within the drawing area and turned so that the front faces of the slab and the blocks are the broad surfaces presented to the viewer. The slab's front face must be tall and broad enough to hold a point well away from all four of its edges, and each block's front face likewise. That gives the annotator room it did not have when those faces rendered as narrow strips.

Targets: numeral 12 is now identified in the interior of the slab's front face, well away from every edge of that face, and numeral 44 in the interior of the middle block's front face on the same terms. Both remain broad interior regions with no midpoint, depth, or quarter modifier, and each part is still named by stable position, so the middle block continues to identify the handle 44.

Length stayed within the limit by compressing lower-risk wording: the band and silhouette sentences say the same thing in fewer words, and the perimeter member 24 target keeps its front-strip region. FIG. 1 is 2799 characters, the other four briefs are unchanged, every declaration matches its sheet list, all 16 numerals remain covered, and no claim, description, drawing description, or numeral definition was touched.

input.summary: Repaired the FIG. 1 endpoint failures for numerals 12 and 44. The slab's front face and each block's front face must now be drawn large enough to hold a point well away from all four edges, the machine is drawn large and turned so those front faces are the broad surfaces presented to the viewer, and both numerals now target the interior of their face well away from every edge. Compressed other wording to keep the brief at 2799 characters. No application text, claim, or numeral definition changed.
reasoning: The report gave raw coordinates showing both dots on boundary lines: numeral 12 by the corner where the slab's front and left faces meet, numeral 44 on the top edge of the middle block's front face. That is a room problem, so the repair had to enlarge the faces as well as reword the targets; repeating 'well inside its front face' would have produced the same cramped region.

The perspective from above and to the front left shows both a front face and a left face on every body, and numeral 12 drifted toward the seam between them. The brief now requires the machine to be turned so that the front faces of the slab and the blocks are the broad surfaces presented to the viewer, which pushes the front face away from the corner where the previous dot landed.

Three blocks side by side made each block's front face short, so numeral 44 had little vertical room and hit the top boundary. Each block is now drawn broad and tall with a front face able to hold a point well away from its edges, which addresses the vertical crowding without changing what the blocks are.

For the target wording I used 'in the interior of its front face, well away from every edge of that face'. That is a broad interior instruction rather than an exact midpoint or depth modifier, so it complies with the endpoint rules while telling the reviewers plainly that an edge-adjacent dot does not satisfy the brief.

I left numerals 18 and 20 reading 'well inside its front face' because they passed and their faces get the same enlargement from the shared block sentence. Rewriting passing targets would have cost characters I needed elsewhere and put certified endpoints back in play.

The enlargements pushed the brief to 2915 characters, so length came out of lower-risk wording: the silhouette sentence for numeral 10, the band sentence, and the perimeter member 24 target, which keeps its front-strip region since the strip is already specified deep enough to hold an interior point. The mounting-location disclaimer for handle 44 was preserved intact because a previous review required it.

All five keys are cited, in the Background only.
